analysis.one_liner: Requires consent before companies sell your personal data or Social Security number.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2003 with no cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required commercial companies to give notice and an opt-out before selling or sharing your personally identifiable information for marketing, and made it a crime to display, sell, or buy someone's Social Security number without their explicit consent. It would also have banned printing Social Security numbers on government checks and driver's licenses, stopped companies from refusing service to people who won't hand over their number, replaced the financial industry's weak opt-out system with a requirement that customers affirmatively agree before their financial data is sold, and barred the sale of protected health information. The Federal Trade Commission, the Justice Department, and state attorneys general would have enforced it.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers. Anyone whose name, address, phone number, or Social Security number is collected and sold would gain the right to stop the sale, and identity thieves, stalkers, and debt collectors would lose their easiest data source. People currently forced to give a Social Security number just to buy goods or services could refuse without being denied the purchase.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers whose data is bought and sold

how_it_helps.text: Commercial entities could not collect personally identifiable information and disclose it to nonaffiliated third parties for marketing, or sell it, without notice and an opportunity for the individual to restrict the disclosure, enforced by the FTC with penalties up to $25,000 per violation [S2][S3].

Displaying, selling, or purchasing a Social Security number without the individual's affirmatively expressed consent would become a federal crime, with civil penalties of up to $5,000 per violation and private lawsuits allowing up to $500 per violation, trebled for willful violations [S2][S3].
Federal, state, and local agencies could not print Social Security numbers on government-issued checks, and states could not display them on driver's licenses or motor vehicle registrations [S2][S3].

A commercial entity could not require a person to provide a Social Security number to buy goods or services, or deny service for refusing, with narrow exceptions such as credit checks and fraud prevention [S2][S3].

The bill would have amended the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act so that financial institutions could not sell or share nonpublic personal financial information with nonaffiliated third parties unless the customer affirmatively consented, replacing the existing opt-out system, and would prohibit the selling or marketing of protected health information [S2][S3].
State attorneys general could sue to enforce the act, and the Driver's Privacy Protection Act would be expanded to cover photographs and copies of driver's licenses [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers, list sellers, and marketers that profit from reselling consumer information; banks, credit card issuers, and other financial institutions that share customer data with outside marketers under the current opt-out system; and businesses that use Social Security numbers as a customer identifier. Compliance and lost data revenue could be passed on to customers.

drawbacks.text: Title I would preempt state privacy law, superseding 'any statutory and common law of States' on the collection and sale of personally identifiable information, which could override stronger state protections already in place [S3].

A safe harbor would exempt companies from liability if they follow self-regulatory guidelines issued by seal programs or the marketing and online industries and approved by the FTC, letting the industry write its own compliance rules [S3].

For general commercial data the bill relies on opt-out rather than requiring consent up front, and it carves out broad exceptions for business-to-business and government interactions involving Social Security numbers, with the Attorney General writing rules to define them [S3].
The consumer transaction limits would sunset six years after taking effect, and class actions to enforce them would be barred, leaving enforcement to regulators and state attorneys general [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections target real, documented harms: the bill's own findings state that the display, sale, and purchase of Social Security numbers contributes to fraud, identity theft, stalking, and other violent crimes [S3]. The compliance burden on business is real but comparable to rules the financial industry already operated under, and the preemption and safe-harbor provisions would have blunted the bill's strength in ways privacy advocates criticized. On balance the consumer protections outweigh the costs, though the design is softer than an outright data-sale ban.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote for the rest of the two-year Congress.

narrative.text: Senator Dianne Feinstein introduced the Privacy Act of 2003 on March 31, 2003, and spoke on its introduction [S1][S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day; no cosponsors signed on [S4][S5].
No further action was ever taken on the bill in the 108th Congress; the record after referral is empty, and the Congress ended January 3, 2005 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers, list sellers, and financial institutions that profit from reselling customer information are better off, because the restrictions never took effect and Social Security numbers and personal data remained legally saleable. Consumers gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; it received no cosponsors

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing or markup, or any further action, before the Congress ended

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never brought the bill to a hearing or markup during the 108th Congress

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held and the bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and a Republican-run committee that took no action.

industries.note: Their business is collecting and reselling personal information; the bill would criminalize selling Social Security numbers without consent and let individuals block the sale of their data. Their gain is consumers' exposure to identity theft and junk marketing.

industries.industry: Banks, credit card issuers, and other financial institutions
industries.note: The bill would convert Gramm-Leach-Bliley's opt-out into affirmative opt-in consent before sharing customer financial data with outside marketers, cutting off a revenue stream built on data customers rarely realize is being shared.
Title IV would prohibit selling or marketing protected health information by specified entities, closing a channel pharmaceutical marketers and data firms use to target patients.

They could still use data to market their own products, but selling customer lists to nonaffiliated third parties would require notice and a lasting opt-out, with an industry-approved self-regulation safe harbor available as a partial cushion.
